title: Container boundaries
summary: Review a container definition for user, version, health, and resource boundaries.

scenario.briefing: The orders API is moving into a container. Review the definition before it reaches the shared two-vCPU server.

objectives.description: Explain reproducible and bounded container practice.

hints: A floating latest tag makes builds unreproducible.
Running as root increases the impact of a compromise.
A health check and resource limits protect the shared host.
Reject until it uses a pinned base, a non-root user, a health check, and CPU/memory limits.

misconceptions.description: Accepting a floating base image tag.
misconceptions.feedback: A floating tag makes the build non-reproducible. Pin a version or digest and rebuild deliberately.

misconceptions.description: Treating container limits as a complete isolation boundary.
misconceptions.feedback: Limits control resource use; the container still shares the host kernel. Pinning, non-root users, and least privilege remain necessary.

sections.title: A container is a process with boundaries
sections.body: Containers package an application and its runtime, but they are not a security boundary by themselves. A pinned base image, non-root user, read-only filesystem where possible, and minimal installed tools reduce risk.

sections.title: Resources must be bounded
sections.body: On a shared server, an unbounded container can starve other services. CPU and memory limits, a health check, and logs with retention turn a dangerous process into an operable one.

vocabulary.definition: The starting filesystem for a container image.
A process account without administrative privileges.
A cap on CPU, memory, or other host resources.

steps.title: Review the container
steps.prompt: Select every supported finding and choose a verdict.

artifact.title: Proposed Dockerfile
artifact.caption: For the orders API on the shared campus host.
artifact.content:
FROM node:latest
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

# No USER, HEALTHCHECK, memory limit, or CPU limit.

findings.label: The node:latest base is not pinned.
The container runs as root by default.
npm install without a lockfile strategy is not reproducible.
The container is safe because it is isolated from the host.

verdicts.label: Reject until the base is pinned, a non-root user is set, installs are reproducible, health is checked, and resources are bounded
Add a version label and ship

steps.explanation: Reproducibility, privilege, install command, health, and resources are all unaddressed. A container still consumes the shared host.
hints: Read the base image tag, the user, and the install step.
Check whether the runtime needs a compiler and package manager.
Check the health probe and what it actually proves.
Reject until the base is pinned, the process is non-root, build tools are absent, and the probe checks the app.

steps.title: Operable containers

statements.label: Pinned base images make builds reproducible.
Running as root increases the impact of a compromise.
Resource limits protect other services on the host.
A container is a complete security boundary by itself.

steps.explanation: Containers improve packaging and deployment; they do not remove the need for privilege, resource, and image controls.
hints: A tag is a moving pointer unless it is a digest or exact version.
The container user is the process user.
Limits bound blast radius but do not replace isolation.
Select pinning, non-root, and limits; reject the claim that containers are isolated by default.
